name: Freya Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brightline Broadband on the business customers desk, so it's shops, cafés and small offices whose internet has gone down. I'm in the contact centre three days a week and at home the other two. I moved over from the home customers team in the spring, so I'm still learning the business contracts, and I ask a lot of questions. The business desk pays a bit more, because when a café's card machine goes down, they're losing money every minute.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The waiting wears me out. I log a fault, book an engineer, and then the café owner rings back every hour asking where the van is, and I don't know. What I like is when you can actually fix it on the call, talk someone through resetting their router and hear the card machine beep back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds plausible, honestly. We've already got a tool that writes a summary after each call, and it's alright. Saves me maybe ten minutes a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's handy, not magic, which is what most of us think already. Online I'd say nothing; I don't really argue about this stuff. With friends I'd probably shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it means my job carries on. Broadband faults are messy, and customers still want someone who'll chase the engineer. I'd be more worried about Brightline's prices going up and customers leaving, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the business desk and get better at the contracts. Sam and I are getting married next summer, so I'd keep the wedding plans as they are, a hundred guests at the cricket club. I'd keep using the summary tool now and then, when I remember.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Sam's an electrician and always busy, we've got nine months saved, and I like my job. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a café owner who's lost a morning's takings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the café owner that I'd ring the engineer myself and call back by twelve. I learned that from Mandy, who sat next to me when I started. A summary tool can write up a broadband call, but it can't promise a panicking café owner that I'll ring back by twelve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said prices worry you more. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, mostly. Every January the bills go up and the business customers ring to cancel. If enough of them leave, the desk gets smaller. That's been true for years, with or without AI.

say: AI is **handy, not magic**, and saves about ten minutes a day.
I wouldn't **argue online** about it; I'd mostly shrug.
think: My **job carries on**, because broadband faults stay messy.
Rising **prices** and customers leaving worry me more than AI.
do: Keep going on the **business desk** and learn the contracts properly.
Keep the **wedding plans** for next summer as they are.
Use the **summary tool** now and then.
feel: **Calm**, with Sam's steady work and nine months saved.
S0.quote: A summary tool can write up a broadband call, but it can't promise a panicking café owner that I'll ring back by twelve.
fieldNote: Freya sees AI as a **small helper**, in line with her steady, wait-for-proof style.
Her real long-running worry is **customers leaving** over prices.
Her **wedding** next summer is the life event she protects in every picture.
She learned the job from a colleague, **Mandy**, and values that kind of learning.

steps.text: Keep learning business contracts on Brightline's business desk
Keep next summer's hundred-guest wedding at the cricket club
Use the call summary tool when it saves time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, answering customers is on the list. That's me, isn't it. My desk would shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see what it actually does before we panic, because that's my style. I'd say companies should give people proper notice and training. That's fair, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm the newest one on the broadband firm's business desk and the slowest on contracts, so if the desk shrinks, it shrinks from my end. I'm not daft about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the AI training Brightline offers, once a couple of people say it's worth it. I'd also ask about the field engineer trainee scheme, because Sam says fibre jobs will be busy for years and it's hands-on. And I'd put the wedding savings on hold and add an extra three hundred a month to the emergency pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. I'm not falling apart, but I'd be checking my emails for anything from HR.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A smaller wedding, maybe. Fifty people, not a hundred, and use the difference as a cushion. Mum would be upset, but she'd get over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Sam feel about you going into engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's dead keen. He reckons I'd be good at it, and there aren't many women doing it so they want more. I'm less sure, I've never climbed a ladder for work.

say: Let's **see what it does** before anyone on the business desk panics.
Companies should give staff **proper notice** and paid training before cutting anyone.
think: I'm the **newest and slowest** on the business desk.
If the desk shrinks, it shrinks **from my end**.
do: Take Brightline's **AI training** once colleagues say it's worth it.
Ask about the **field engineer** trainee scheme.
Add **£300 a month** to the emergency pot.
feel: **Anxious**, checking emails for anything from HR.
Unsure about **climbing ladders** for work, despite Sam's encouragement.
S1.quote: I'm the newest one on the broadband firm's business desk and the slowest on contracts, so if the desk shrinks, it shrinks from my end.
fieldNote: Freya expects cuts to fall on **the newest staff**, including her.
Her plan mixes **learning AI** and a move into **hands-on** fibre work.
She'd shrink the **wedding** from a hundred guests to fifty to build a cushion.
Partner **Sam** pushes her toward the trade more than she pushes herself.

steps.text: Take Brightline's AI training once colleagues rate it
Apply for Brightline's field engineer trainee scheme
Add £300 a month to the emergency pot
Cut the wedding from a hundred guests to fifty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Two years. That's the business desk gone, and the home desk, and probably the whole contact centre. Sam's work would carry on until the robots, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, and fast, something sensible like paying people while they retrain. I wouldn't be on the barricades, but I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose my job at the broadband firm, I think within the first year. There's no version of answering phones that survives a machine that does it better and cheaper. I'd have to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an electrical apprenticeship straight away, maybe working alongside Sam if his boss would have me. We'd shrink the wedding to the registry office and a meal. I'd stop the takeaways and the gym, and live off Sam's wage while I trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Not for money right now, but for the next ten years. I don't know what work looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come three years later. What does that mean for you and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots coming three years later means Sam's job lasts until about 2031, then who knows. So we'd be a family of two people learning the same trade that's also on a clock. That's what keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still get married next summer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want the day. Just smaller. Mum would cry either way.

say: We need a **sensible government plan**, like paying people while they retrain.
I'd **vote** for whoever has a real plan.
think: I'd **lose my job** at Brightline within the first year.
Answering phones can't survive a machine that's **better and cheaper**.
do: Start an **electrical apprenticeship**, ideally alongside Sam.
Shrink the wedding to a **registry office** and a meal.
Stop **takeaways and the gym** and live on Sam's wage while training.
feel: **Scared** about the next ten years rather than about money today.
S2.quote: I'd lose my job at the broadband firm, I think within the first year. There's no version of answering phones that survives a machine that does it better and cheaper.
fieldNote: Freya expects to **lose her job** and says so plainly.
She'd follow Sam into the **electrical trade**, knowing robots follow by 2031.
The whole household would rely on **one hands-on trade** with a clock on it.
She'd **still marry**, just smaller.

steps.text: Start an electrical apprenticeship alongside Sam
Hold the wedding at the registry office with a meal
Stop takeaways and the gym and live on Sam's wage
Vote for whichever party has a retraining plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two. That's enough to do something properly, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when you start planning, not when you start panicking. I'd tell the newer ones on the desk to get training while Brightline is still paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the desk goes around 2031, and I go with it. But I'd want to have moved before then. Five years is time to learn a trade properly, not just grab one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd apply for Brightline's fibre engineer training, which pays while you learn. I'd do the AI course too, because the engineers use apps to log jobs, and I'd want to be quick with that. We'd keep the wedding as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but OK. It's like getting a long warning on a weather app. You still have to deal with the storm, but you've got time to bring the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2034. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots that can do fibre work come around 2034, so even the fibre engineer job I'd train for has a clock on it. But I'd have experience by then, and maybe I'd be supervising the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the desk would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mandy, definitely. She's forty-nine and she's been on the phones at Brightline twenty years. I'd want to drag her onto a course with me.

say: Newer staff should get **training** while Brightline still pays for it.
think: The desk goes **around 2031**, and I'd go with it.
Five years is enough to learn a **trade properly**.
do: Apply for Brightline's **fibre engineer training**, paid while learning.
Take the **AI course** to handle engineers' job apps.
feel: **Nervous but OK**, with time to prepare.
Worried for colleagues like **Mandy**, twenty years on the phones.
S3.quote: Robots that can do fibre work come around 2034, so even the fibre engineer job I'd train for has a clock on it.
fieldNote: Freya stays anxious because she still expects the **desk to go**.
Five years turns her move into a **planned trade**, paid for by Brightline.
She sees she might end up **supervising robots** later.
Her concern for **older colleagues** comes through clearly.

steps.text: Apply for Brightline's paid fibre engineer training
Take the AI course for engineers' job-logging apps
Keep the wedding at the cricket club as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, that's a lot. I'd be thirty-seven, married, maybe with kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's do this sensibly. Training, notice, a bit of help from the government. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be gone from the phones by then anyway, probably. I don't see myself doing this at thirty-seven. So it's more about choosing the next thing well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the business desk for now and get good at it. I'd use the AI tools more as they get better. In two or three years I'd decide between the engineer route and a team leader job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. With ten years' warning, AI stops being a threat and becomes just one more thing to plan around, like the wedding and kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see kids in the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. We'd try for a baby a couple of years after the wedding. Ten years' warning makes that easier, not harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still bothers you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's job, mostly. Robots for electrical work around 2039 would hit him at forty. But that's a long way off.

say: There's **time**, so let's handle it **sensibly** at work and at home.
Training, notice and a bit of **government help** would be enough, nothing dramatic.
think: I'd probably have **left the phones** by thirty-seven anyway, whatever AI does.
It's really about **choosing** my next job well, not about losing this one.
do: Stay on the **business desk** for now and get good at it.
Use **AI tools** more as they improve.
Decide between **engineer** and **team leader** in two or three years.
feel: **Fine**, with AI as one more thing to plan around.
A small worry about **Sam's job** around 2039.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, AI stops being a threat and becomes just one more thing to plan around, like the wedding and kids.
fieldNote: With ten years, Freya's mood drops to **uneasy**, her lowest after AI Plateau.
She'd decide on a path in **two or three years**, true to her steady style.
**Kids after the wedding** stay on track.
Her lingering worry shifts to **Sam's trade** around 2039.

steps.text: Stay on Brightline's business desk and master the contracts
Use the AI tools more as they improve
Decide between engineer and team leader in two or three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Me and Sam both on a clock at the same time, with a wedding and maybe kids. What would help is being paid while I retrain, and Brightline offering its own staff the engineer places first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. It's not just my job, it's our two jobs together. Most people think about AI and their own job, but my fiancé Sam and I would be two people betting our whole house on the same trade.

headlineQuote: Most people think about AI and their own job, but my fiancé Sam and I would be two people betting our whole house on the same trade.
portrait: Freya, **27**, is new to Brightline Broadband's **business desk**, after starting on home customers.
She uses AI **now and then** and waits for colleagues to prove a tool first.
She lives with **Sam**, an electrician, and they're marrying next summer.
She's **calm** in AI Plateau but alarmed in fast AGI, expecting to lose her job.
Her plan is a **hands-on trade**, with the wedding scaled to fit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with her and Sam both on a **clock** at once.
whatWouldHelp: Being **paid to retrain**, with Brightline offering staff the **engineer** places first.
